asparagus.description_seasoned: Asparagus (Asparagus officinalis) is a long-lived herbaceous perennial grown for the tender spring spears it pushes from a deep, cold-hardy crown. Established once from one-year-old crowns in a deep trench, a well-sited bed yields for 15 to 20 years and sometimes far longer. The rhythm is fixed: spears emerge as the soil warms and are cut for a spring window that lengthens with bed age, reaching six to ten weeks on a mature crown, after which every remaining spear grows into a tall fern canopy that recharges the crown for the next season. Its physiology is temperate rather than tropical. UC IPM ties the plant's longevity to getting a true dormant season each year, not just a mild pause, so a bed set where winter never really arrives will not hold. Variety choice sets the ceiling. All-male hybrids outyield the open-pollinated types and skip the weedy volunteer seedlings: Millennium, a cold-hardy University of Guelph hybrid, is the modern high-yield northern standard but runs more susceptible to rust, while the Rutgers Jersey hybrids, represented here by Jersey Knight, carry the class's vigor-based field tolerance to rust and to Fusarium crown and root rot. Among the open-pollinated types, Mary Washington is the century-old heirloom standard, hardy but lighter-yielding with mixed male and female plants, and Purple Passion is a sweeter, purple-speared strain that yields less and catches foliage disease more easily. Give asparagus full sun and deep, well-drained ground, and choose the site with care, since the crowns will hold it for two decades.
asparagus.hardiness_notes_seasoned: The distinction that matters is crown versus top growth: the crown is deeply cold-hardy and overwinters dormant in the ground, riding out hard freezes, while the ferns and emerged spears are frost-tender. Missouri's guidance is reassuring on what a late freeze actually costs you: the spears standing at the time can be ruined, but the crown below is untouched and the rest of the season's cutting comes in normally. At the other end of the year, it is the first fall frost that sends the ferns into dieback. The dormancy in between is a requirement, not just something the plant puts up with. UC IPM treats the dormant stretch as one half of what the plant needs each year, since the crown does its rebuilding while the top is down, so a site that never truly cools leaves that recharge unfinished and the bed thins out over the years. That is why this belongs to temperate gardens rather than tropical ones. In the coldest, snow-poor winters, mulch the crowns, since the least cold-hardy types can injure in a deep freeze without snow cover.
asparagus.soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Give asparagus a deep, fertile, well-drained bed rich in organic matter and sited in full sun. Texture is not the real constraint here, drainage is. The University of Minnesota accepts anything from heavy clay to light sand provided water keeps moving through it instead of standing after a rain, and Michigan State puts a hard edge on the same point: if water sits in the spot for even an hour, the site is too wet. A deep sandy loam is the classic asparagus soil because it drains freely and lets you dig the planting trench. Work in generous compost and clear perennial weeds before planting, because the crowns will hold that ground for 15 to 20 years.

beet.regions.utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: In St. George's Dixie, sow beets direct in early March for a spring crop pulled by mid-May, before the real summer heat sets in. The bed then sits idle through June, since St. George routinely tops 100°F that month. Sow again from July 1 to August 1 for a fall crop. There is no need to clear the whole row at once: USU Extension's fall guidance for this county has the roots keeping in cold ground, so dig beets as you want them right through the winter, long past the first frost around November 1.

carrot.regions.utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: In St. George's Dixie, sow carrots direct in early March for a spring crop pulled by late May, before the summer heat sets in. The bed then sits idle through June, since St. George routinely tops 100°F that month. Sow again in July for a fall crop. Leave that row standing when the weather turns cold. USU Extension counts the winter bed as its own storage for carrots here, so pull them a few at a time whenever you want them, well past the first frost around November 1.

turnip.regions.utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: In St. George's Dixie, sow turnips direct in mid-February for a spring crop pulled by late April, before the heat builds. The bed then sits idle through May and June, since St. George routinely tops 100°F in June. Sow again from July 1 to August 1 for a fall crop. Frost does not end this one. USU Extension has turnip roots holding where they grew once the cold arrives, so keep digging through the winter months, well past the first frost around November 1.

spring-onion.regions.utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: St. George grows green onions on two direct-sown cycles, and USU Extension's fall-gardening guidance for the area supports both on the same logic: the crop finishes fast enough that there is room for a sowing at each end of the season. The spring sowing runs from about Feb 15, USU's St. George Group A date for onions, with a quick harvest by late April. St. George's low desert heats up fast each spring and reaches 100°F in June, July, and August, so sowing pauses from May until a second sowing from about Aug 1 to Aug 20 restarts the crop once that heat begins to ease, cropping from late September up to the Nov 1 first frost, which a light touch sweetens but a hard freeze ends. Unlike the bulbing storage onion, green onion is harvested young and carries no day-length restriction.

cabbage.regions.hawaii_tropical.resolved_by_zone: Cabbage is marginal in lowland tropical Hawaii and belongs to the cool season. CTAHR divides the state by elevation: cool high-elevation ground carries a cabbage crop in any month, while down at low elevation the crop works only across the winter. The low-elevation winter window (about October to November transplant) is modeled because the cited CTAHR bulletin B-91 is a scanned PDF that did not parse and does not table cabbage months. Harvest months derived.

cabbage.regions.hawaii_tropical.region_notes_sea: Cabbage is marginal in tropical lowland Hawaii. CTAHR divides the state by elevation: cool high-elevation ground carries a cabbage crop in any month, though leaf diseases become the main worry there, while at low elevation it is a winter crop only. The low-elevation cool-season window is modeled on that qualitative guidance, since the cited CTAHR Bulletin B-91 is a scanned PDF that did not parse and does not list cabbage months directly. Treat the window and the derived harvest as a modeled estimate pending a parseable modern CTAHR source.

Chill is never the limiter here: the belt delivers roughly 1100 to 1500 chilling hours a year in zone 7, clearing this crop's variety range with margin (NC State Extension; regional four-source chill basket). What limits it is bloom and harvest weather, and NC State is direct about the odds: even on a site that suits them, cherries and apricots are trees that skip crops in some years and that repay close management rather than running themselves. Cherries bloom early enough to meet a late freeze, and rain at ripening splits the fruit and invites brown rot, both of which run harder on the humid Piedmont and Coastal Plain than in the mountains. That said, sour cherry's own characteristics tilt the odds toward a crop: NC State notes the sour types are the hardier of the two cherries, and that sour cherry is self fertile while sweet cherry needs a second variety to pollinate, so a single tree can set fruit on its own. It also carries the belt's humidity better than sweet and ripens quickly, shortening its exposure to harvest rain. Treat it as the cherry to choose here and expect fruit in good years rather than every year.

chives.regions.fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginn: On the Florida peninsula (zones 10 and 11), chives are a cool-season herb. Plant in fall and cut from the clump through the mild winter and into spring, which UF/IFAS names as the plant's best stretch in Florida. Summer is the hard part. Heat and humidity push chives into a rest, so give the plant afternoon shade, keep it watered, and let it pick back up as things cool off.

echinacea.regions.fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginn: In peninsular Florida (zones 10 to 11), coneflowers can bloom from spring into late fall, but they often do not last long. Florida's extension experts warn that a coneflower here may only be a two-season plant, and that drainage is usually what decides which way it goes. Plant in late winter in full sun and the best-draining soil you can, keep it lean, and stick with the plain, tough kinds. Be ready to replant, since it may not come back for years the way it does up north.

english-cucumber.diseases[1].symptoms_seasoned: Angular yellow blotches bounded by the leaf veins appear on the upper surface, with a grayish or purplish fuzzy growth beneath in humid weather. Spots brown and run together, and severe infection rapidly defoliates the vines. Of the foliage diseases that hit cucumbers and their relatives, this is the one that costs growers the most, and the high humidity under cover can drive it hard.

fig.companions.bad_seasoned[0].why_seasoned: Do not plant a fig into sandy soil known to carry heavy root-knot nematode populations, or straight into ground where a nematode-declined fig was just removed. In warm sandy regions nothing else takes down as many fig trees, and because figs grow on their own roots there is no resistant rootstock to fall back on the way there is for stone fruit. The fix is site selection, not a companion plant: choose the best-drained, least infested ground, or replace a generous volume of soil.

lime.diseases[5].cause_seasoned: The fungus Colletotrichum acutatum infects open flowers during rainy, humid conditions, causing the young fruit to abscise. The damage therefore lands only where wet weather and open bloom coincide.

pawpaw.pests[0].cause_seasoned: Larvae of the pawpaw peduncle borer (Talponia plummeriana), a small moth. At roughly 5 millimeters the larva is easy to miss, and the feeding happens out of sight inside the flower itself, so the first sign is a bloom that dies back and drops instead of setting fruit. How much of the bloom you lose swings widely from one season to the next.

raspberry.regions.utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: Raspberry is marginal in the St. George Dixie core: this is a hot, low, alkaline-soil site, the kind Utah State University Extension flags as difficult for the crop, while the county's dependable raspberry ground is its higher-elevation towns above the valley. The steer here is toward heat-tolerant, low-chill, fall-bearing (primocane) types, and USU Extension's reasoning is a timing one: a primocane crop comes in on the far side of the summer peak, late enough that the fruit is not sitting through the worst of the desert sun, which is what scorches a summer-bearing crop. Look to the fall-bearing varieties Caroline, Josephine, Polana, Joan J, and Polka, or the low-chill desert canes Bababerry and Dorman Red. Plant dormant canes in late winter, and expect the alkaline soil to drive iron chlorosis, so treat yellowing leaves with a chelated iron. Give the planting afternoon shade to cut sunburn, mulch the shallow roots, use raised beds in heavy soil, and water steadily through the dry heat. Even managed well, treat this as a hard-won, shorter-lived planting than a cooler climate would give.

strawberry.regions.ca_north_coast.region_notes_seas: On California's cool, foggy north and central coast (zones 9 and 10, Monterey County north), strawberries are grown as a fall-planted annual system rather than a long-lived perennial bed. Set short-day (June-bearing) transplants from mid August through the fall, a window that holds up and down the coast, and day-neutral types from late September into November. The first full season after planting is the best one this system gives you, and every year after it returns less, so the bed gets pulled and reset rather than carried forward. The cool maritime climate puts little heat stress on fruit set, the main flush builds to heaviest production in May and June, and day-neutral varieties can fruit across much of the year on the mild coast. Hard frost is rare, but protect open blossoms in any inland cold pocket. Grow on raised, well-drained beds and keep moisture off the flowers to limit fruit rot in the damp coastal air.
